content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new data reconstruction attack in federated learning. The key idea is using the Frobenius norm to ignore the required knowledge of the learning rate in deep gradient leakage (DGL) attacks. Experimental results were conducted on three benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, showing that the proposed attack achieves better reconstruction accuracy than DGL attacks. The paper also presents the results of the attacks under DP and model sparsification (defenses).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The research topic is significant. However, there are several weaknesses in the current form of the paper.

- The threat model is unclear or even unrealistic. How could the adversary gain the client's local weights transmitted to the server? Is the adversary a compromised client or the server? If the adversary is a compromised client, the threat model becomes unrealistic. If the adversary is the server, then the threat model and the proposed attack does not advance our knowledge about data reconstruction attacks compared with existing works, such as [1, 2]. In [2], a server can reconstruct a large portion of clients' local data compared with only 50 images used in the experiment of this paper. I am not sure why only 50 images are used.

- Regarding the proposed data reconstruction attack, how could the adversary compute the $\rVert \triangledown_{W^t}\mathcal{L}(x^*, y^*) \lVert$_F given the model parameter $W^t$ without any information about the learning rate $\alpha$ used in the previous iteration? In addition, Eq. 10 is a slight modification of DLG to be similar to the proposed attacks. It clearly shows that the proposed attack is incremental. The paper claims that the proposed attack enlarges the search margin and increases the probability of recovering the original data without any theoretical analysis or guarantees. Some empirical results cannot justify this claim and shed light on understanding the effectiveness of the tuning factor. How to select or optimize the tuning parameters?

- Experimental results are unconvincing. More complex datasets are needed, such as ImageNet, CelebA, etc., to clearly show the clear advantages of the proposed attacks. 10 clients, each of whom has a 10% IID partition of the data, is not a realistic experimental setting in FL. Baseline approaches are out-of-date, and more recently developed attacks such as [2] are needed.

- The defenses are incorrect. What is the level of DP protection when the paper clips the model weights and injects the noise? What is the advantage of doing so? In my experience, simply injecting the DP-preserving noise without considering the level of privacy risk bounded by a privacy budget does not provide any protection. In addition, to defend against data reconstruction attacks, local DP should be a better countermeasure than DP, as applied in the paper. In short, the experiments do not advance my knowledge about data reconstruction attacks and defenses in FL. 

[1] [Nasr et al., 2019] Comprehensive privacy analysis of deep learning: Passive and active white-box inference attacks against centralized and federated learning. In 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, SP 2019, San Francisco, CA, USA, May 19-23, 2019, pages 739–753. IEEE.

[2] [Boenisch et al., 2021] WHEN THE CURIOUS ABANDON HONESTY: FEDERATED LEARNING IS NOT PRIVATE.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written. However, the novelty is very limited. The technical contribution is incremental compared with existing attacks. The attacks can be reproduced with some effort.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper studies an important problem. However, there is room for improvement. The paper in its current form does not offer a fundamental advantage in data reconstruction attacks and defenses in FL. Please see my detailed comments above.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses the topic of leakage of data while training models in a Federated Learning setup. Recent work has shown that individual data samples can be reconstructed from access to (aggregated) model gradients. For images, the idea is to start by a random estimate of the pixels, express the gradient as a differentiable function of the image and do SGD on the pixel space to match the gradient of the candidate sample to the model update received through FL. This paper proposes two refinements to this method:
- DLM: match the candidate gradient to an update scaled by a factor of gamma
- DLM+: match the normalized candidate gradient to the normalized update.

The authors evaluate both methods on three datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) and two types of architectures (MLP and LeNet). Experiments show the superiority of their method over competing alternatives (DLG, cosine). Further experiments also show that differential privacy and model sparsification are effective counter-measures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 
- The proposed method (DLM+) improves the average PSNR (from the best baseline of 39.99 to 46.96)
- The authors evaluate empirically the effect of known leakage mitigations. In particular, for Differential Privacy, it is interesting to see that relatively mild noise is sufficient to decrease PSNR while the theoretical guarantees of DP require higher levels of noise. 

Weaknesses
- DLM/DLM+ are a simple modifications of existing methods
- Accuracy and SSIM are very similar to the baselines (respectively 90%->92% and 0.91->0.92). This is surprising given the large difference in average PSNR and seems to indicate that the gains are not that impressive.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In my opinion, the paper is clearly written and of good quality (comparison to the right baselines, extensive experiments). However, I do not think that the method is very original, it is a variant of existing methods (DLG, cosine). The work seems reproducible from information in the paper, although I have not looked at the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is overall well-written but provides the technical contribution is light, and the improvement over competing alternatives is not clear-cut (better on PSNR but similar on SSIM and ACC).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies privacy leakage in federated learning. Unlike existing methods focusing on using the shared gradients (e.g., FedSGD), the proposed method focuses on using the shared model parameters (e.g., FedAvg). Specifically, the authors present two frameworks, called DLM and DLM+, to demonstrate that transmitting model weights is also likely to leak private local data of clients, by avoiding auxiliary information such as weights, optimizers, etc. Evaluations show the generality of the proposed attack frameworks. The authors also adopt two existing defenses, i.e., differential privacy and model sparsification, to defend the proposed attacks and show that the defenses are not effective enough.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
+ The studied problem is important
+ Paper is easy to follow in general

Weaknesses
- Novelty is limited
- Experimental setup is unclear
- Evaluation is insufficient
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The main idea is to change the gradient matching in the existing attacks to FedSGD to the parameter matching to FedAvg. This idea is straightforward and I do not see any significant contribution here.  

In the considered attack scenario, the attacker is assumed to know the loss function, which is impractical. Existing attacks to FedSGD do not have this assumption. 

Is the proposed attack convergent? How to setup the different learning rates in practice? 

How many samples are recovered? What batch size is used? In what round the proposed attack recovers the image?  

There exist many advanced deep leakage from gradient attacks to FL,  e.g., . 

Yin et al., See through gradients: Image batch recovery via gradinversion. In CVPR, 2021
Jeon et al., Gradient inversion with generative image prior. In NeurIPS, 2021
Balunovic et al., Bayesian Framework for Gradient Leakage. In ICLR, 2022
Fowl et al., Robbing the Fed: Directly Obtaining Private Data in Federated Learning with Modified Models. In ICLR, 2022

The authors need to discuss and compare with them as well. 


The following paper actually studies the same problem, but the authors do not mention it. 

Dimitrov et al., Data Leakage in Federated Averaging, arXiv 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed attack mainly borrows the idea from the existing attack methods, hence the novelty is narrow. The authors also missed many relevant papers and do not discussion and compare with them.

content.title: Deep Leakage from Model in Federated Learning
content.abstract: Distributed machine learning has been widely used in recent years to tackle large and complex dataset problems. Therewith, the security of distributed learning has also drawn increasing attention from both academia and industry. In this context, federated learning (FL) was developed as a “secure” distributed learning by maintaining private training data locally and only public model gradients are communicated between. However, to date, a variety of gradient leakage attacks have been proposed for this procedure and prove that it is insecure. For instance, a common drawback of these attacks is shared: {they require} too much auxiliary information such as model weights, optimizers, and some hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate), which are difficult to obtain in real situations. Moreover, many existing algorithms avoid transmitting model gradients in FL and turn to sending model weights, such as FedAvg, but few people consider its security breach. In this paper, we present two novel frameworks to demonstrate that transmitting model weights is also likely to leak private local data of clients, i.e., (DLM and DLM+), under the FL scenario. In addition, a variety of experiments are performed to illustrate the effect and generality of our attack frameworks. At the end of this paper, we also introduce two defenses to the proposed attacks and evaluate their protective effects. Comprehensively, the proposed attack and defense schemes can be applied to the generally distributed learning scenario as well, just with some appropriate customization.
